issues.issue: The opening paragraph names "the University of Pennsylvania" as "Recipient," not the Trustees of the University of Pennsylvania (the contracting legal entity, hand-inserted on the face of the document), leaving in doubt which institution, if any, is bound alongside Dr. June. The defect is in this paragraph's own identification of the party.

The stated purpose - use "in a collaborative research study" - is nowhere defined or bounded, and paragraph 6's joint-publication duty attaches only to work "that result[s] from the collaborative research study." Whether Penn's later work falls inside or outside that undefined study turns on this phrase.

"Material" is defined to include "any progeny, portions, unmodified derivatives and any accompanying know-how or data," but paragraph 3 authorizes the Recipient to create a modified lentiviral construct from it, so whether that construct and its progeny are themselves "Material" is unresolved by the definition. The ambiguity is in the words "unmodified derivatives" and "know-how or data" as against what the Recipient was licensed to make.

The flat bar on transferring or making the Material "available to any other person or third party" cannot be squared with the parties' 2007 Materials Transfer Agreement, paragraph 3(i)-(ii), which permits the same materials to be taken to another institution or given to a commercial entity with St. Jude's written consent. Which regime governs after October 2, 2007 - supersession or coexistence - is the disputed point.

The confinement of use to a lentiviral construct "to be used in pre-clinical studies" cannot be squared with the 2007 Materials Transfer Agreement, paragraph 3, which expressly authorizes the Recipient to make a GMP lentiviral vector from the same materials for a Phase I clinical trial. Whether the 2003 pre-clinical limit continued to bind the construct made under it is precisely what the two documents leave open.

"The Material may not be used in humans" cannot be squared with the 2007 Materials Transfer Agreement, paragraph 3, under which St. Jude supplied the same anti-CD19 construct for a Phase I clinical trial in the Recipient's clinical facilities. Whether the 2003 human-use ban survived, and whether it reached the derived vector, is the conflict.

"The Material will not be used for any commercial purpose" is irreconcilable with paragraph 8, which contemplates that the Recipient may commercialize a product containing Material with St. Jude's prior written approval and may patent inventions made through its use. One provision forbids absolutely what the other permits on condition.

The clause is missing its verb ("any publications ... using the Material be jointly published") and conditions the duty on the undefined standard of "academic standards," so neither the mandatory force of the obligation nor what joint publication requires (co-authorship? acknowledgment? approval?) is fixed. Both defects lie in these words.

The joint-publication duty cannot be squared with the publication regime of the 2007 Materials Transfer Agreement, paragraphs 4 and 5, which require only that St. Jude receive a copy, be acknowledged as source, and get thirty days' pre-submission review. Whether the later, lesser publication terms displace the 2003 joint-publication promise is open.

Termination on thirty days' notice requires the Recipient only to "destroy all unused Materials," with no survival clause and no definition of "unused" - leaving unresolved whether already-used Material, progeny and the derived construct may be retained and whether paragraphs 4, 6 and 8 continue to bind after termination. The gap is in this paragraph's own words.

Permitting the Recipient to commercialize with prior written approval and to patent inventions made through use of the Material conflicts with paragraph 4's absolute "will not be used for any commercial purpose" and with paragraph 1's statement that no express or implied licenses or other rights are provided. The three cannot all be given full effect.

The paragraph carries a garbled handwritten interlineation about inventorship "according to US patent law" and a mistyped grant of a "raw-exclusive" (non-exclusive) license, so both the ownership rule and the scope of St. Jude's license are uncertain on the face of the text. Whether the manuscript addition is part of the bargain at all is itself in doubt.

The exculpation is undone only where Claims are "solely caused by the gross negligence or willful misconduct of St. Jude," a carve-out whose "solely" has no stated meaning where causes are mixed. The provision also assigns "all liability" to Recipient without defining the excepted "extent prohibited by law."

Acceptance is expressed to require both the Recipient Scientist's signature and that of "an authorized official of Recipient," yet the executed instrument bears only Dr. June's signature, so whether the institution ever became a party is left open by this sentence. The condition of assent is stated but not satisfied on the face of the document.
